## A Cloud Is a Temporary Agreement

My grandfather could name a cloud the way other people named relatives.

Thin, wispy ones were dinosaur bones. Tall, ragged ones were storms with important business. Low gray clouds were grandmothers who had decided not to visit. Fog was a cloud that couldn’t decide where it was going.

He spoke of the sky as if it were a village: *That one keeps to the north. That dark one travels too fast. See how the smaller clouds gather around it? They’re worried.*

I believed, for a long time, that naming a cloud fixed it in place. A cloud called a thunderhead had a job. A cloud called a sunset was beautiful on purpose. Rain was only rain.

Adults often confuse a category with a destiny. We call a person angry, lonely, difficult, and then behave as though the name were the whole size of them. The sky gets the same treatment from us. We classify the magnificent and the ordinary, then forget that both are busy becoming.

Meteorologists know better, or at least know more. They measure the height at which water gathers, the temperature required for a visible droplet, the forces turning invisible moisture into towers, curtains, and anvils. Satellites look down from orbit and paint clouds in false colors so that their heights and temperatures can be read.

And still we look up and see elephants, feathers, waves, enormous fists.

Perhaps that is not ignorance. Perhaps it is a refusal to let the measurable be the whole truth. A cloud’s shape is not a thing, exactly. It is a verb happening slowly.

I have always liked summer evenings when the heat loosens the horizon. The buildings seem to gather a faint gray haze around their shoulders. Rooftops disappear first, then towers, until the city appears to be trying on weather larger than itself. Sometimes the upper floors vanish entirely. You imagine invisible rooms up there, filled with lamps and quiet clocks.

The air has begun negotiating with itself.

Water rises from the grass, the pavement, the laundry, the river. It rises invisibly into the warmth. Then, at the perfect height, thousands of tiny reasons agree to become visible.

That agreement does not last. The cloud shifts, thins, scatters, wanders across the county, becomes a different cloud—or no longer a cloud at all. Nothing in the sky is committed to being what it currently appears to be.

On clear nights I still catch myself looking for names. *Cirrus. Cumulus. Stratus.* The words arrive automatically, neat little boxes drawn around unruly weather.

But sometimes I forget them.

And the sky becomes wonderfully excessive: enormous, unfinished, indifferent to my vocabulary. A whale hangs over the rooftops. A cathedral burns without consuming anything. A mountain of white light turns slowly, showing me one silver face, then another.

For a little while, it makes a shape out of almost disappearing.

A cloud is a temporary agreement among droplets. They gather. They borrow an outline. They hold together long enough for the sun to give them a silver rim, for an airplane to write a temporary sentence across them, for someone standing in a garden to look up and feel briefly, usefully small.

Then they let go.

That is not a sad ending. It is the only way any of us could travel so far overhead.

Tonight I watched a cloud I could not name. It did not need me. It was simply weather, passing through the world, changing, enormous, gone before I had finished describing it.
